transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2028-01-09 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood CSM), Dr. Priya Raman (CTO, Solstice), Evan Zhao (ML Eng), Maya Lopez (SRE)

Summary:
Redwood and Solstice reviewed week-3 POC benchmark delta vs incumbent (LegacyAI). Main focuses: p50/p95/p99 latency deltas, throughput under 95th percentile traffic bursts, KV cache hit behavior, and quantized model tradeoffs. Customer requested a short on-prem quantized run and a CSV with per-route latency buckets. Security questions around KMS and audit logs remain open.

Topics:
- Bench delta readout vs LegacyAI baseline
- Routing/fallback behavior under slot exhaustion
- Quantization effects on tail latency
- KV cache warmup and cache sharding
- Compliance pointers: SOC2/Audit, KMS integration, VPC peering

Action items (recap in call): see metadata action_items

Transcript body:
[00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Priya Raman: Hi, Priya here, Evan and Maya are on too.
[00:17] Liam Carter: Great. We'll jump straight to the bench deltas from the lab. Sofia, do you want to take us through the numbers?
[00:27] Sofia Alvarez: Yeah, sure. So uh this week we ran the head-to-head against LegacyAI using your sample traffic and the new quant profile Q2. The p50's roughly identical, p95 is about 18% better on Redwood for the long prompt set, p99 is a bit noisier - around 10 to 12% improvement but with some spikes when KV cache miss rate rose.
[00:50] Evan Zhao: Wait, the p99 spikes - are those correlated with cold KV cache or when the bigger embeddings are fetched?
[01:00] Sofia Alvarez: Mostly KV warmup. We saw cache misses at the start of a burst because your traffic has a lot of unique session prefixes. The continuous batching helps overall throughput but it doesn't mask first-window misses.
[01:18] Maya Lopez: When you say "KV warmup" do you mean the key-value cache on the model or some layer in our app? I'm sorry, terminology mix.
[01:27] Sofia Alvarez: No worries. The KV I'm referring to is the model-kv cache -- like token-level past key-values. On longer chats, if requests route to a different replica that doesn't have the prefix cached, you see the tail latency bump.
[01:46] Priya Raman: That's essentially our biggest concern - tail latency during bursts. LegacyAI had a hack where they pinned sessions to instances. Is that something Redwood can replicate or do you prefer routing/fallback policies?
[01:59] Liam Carter: We have a couple of levers. Pinning is possible in Dedicated pools but it's heavy. We usually recommend sticky routing for session affinity plus a small prefix cache on the load path. Also, we can tune autoscaling thresholds so you don't hit slot exhaustion.
[02:18] Evan Zhao: The numbers for throughput - you mentioned continuous batching helped. What were the throughput numbers vs baseline at 95% CPU/GPU utilization?
[02:28] Sofia Alvarez: We measured sustained throughput about 22% higher in the Redwood pipeline for the quantized variant on the same hardware profile (A100-equivalent). The dedupe and prefix caching reduced duplicate tokens; your median token cost also dropped.
[02:41] Maya Lopez: Is that with KV caching enabled? Because if caching is disabled in our environment due to privacy concerns, numbers will change.
[02:50] Sofia Alvarez: Right, so we ran two configs. Cache-on gave the 22% throughput delta; cache-off still had a 9-10% throughput uplift over LegacyAI due to kernel selection and batching. So you still get improvement even without KV cache.
[03:06] Priya Raman: On privacy, our security team is strict. We need to know how cache persistence works and encryption at rest. Can you quickly summarize?
[03:15] Ravi Patel: Sure - briefly: caches are ephemeral per-replica by default and never written to persistent disk. If you use our Private (VPC) or on-prem deployment, you get full customer control of KMS for any persisted artifacts. We'll send the security doc with SOC2 references.
[03:29] Priya Raman: Good. Please send that.
[03:31] Liam Carter: Noted. Sofia, back to bench: were there any specific prompt shapes that drove the p99 spikes?
[03:39] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, the long-context prompt set with multi-document summarization had the worst tail. Also when the batcher hit a mix of short and long sequences, long sequences pushed the KV misses. We can tweak batching windowing to group similar lengths, but that trades off latency for short queries.
[03:58] Evan Zhao: Could a quantized 4-bit run exacerbate the tail? We're measuring some quality drift in a couple of samples; would that be visible in the bench?
[04:08] Sofia Alvarez: Quant can sometimes increase compute variability but in our runs the tail was slightly lower for quant due to smaller memory footprint and better cache residency. The quality checks we ran on your eval set showed negligible regression for Q2, but we flagged 3 samples for manual review.
[04:26] Priya Raman: We need that sample list.
[04:28] Liam Carter: We'll include the three flagged prompts in the CSV.
[04:30] Maya Lopez: On routing: earlier you mentioned fallback to a smaller model when capacity is constrained. How does the quality control happen? We don't want hallucinations.
[04:40] Sofia Alvarez: Good question. We have a fallback policy that maps routes to a compatible model family. The platform includes a safety layer — we run a lightweight reranker and threshold check; if the smaller model's score is below the threshold, Redwood will either queue the request briefly (within SLO) or return a degraded response with a metadata tag so you can handle it.
[04:58] Priya Raman: Can you add metadata tagging to our integration so we can monitor per-route quality?
[05:04] Liam Carter: Yes, we can expose per-response quality tags and an error code surface for degraded responses. We'll include the schema in the artifact we send.
[05:12] Evan Zhao: On the on-prem smoke run — what do you need from us?
[05:16] Sofia Alvarez: We'll need a small VM with the same GPU profile, your traffic sample tarball (we can redact PII), and a short window (~10k tokens) to run the quantized binary. We'll return logs and p95/p99.
[05:27] Maya Lopez: We can provide a trimmed traffic sample. I'll prepare it and check data redaction with Priya.
[05:33] Priya Raman: We'll aim to send that by Friday.
[05:36] Liam Carter: Great. A couple of items we should call out: we observed per-route variance where one of your endpoints (the claims-summary) had a 30% higher compute foot print due to longer context and extra embedding fetches. We recommend breaking that route into two—pre-filter then summarize.
[05:52] Evan Zhao: That route is messy, agreed. We'll try to refactor in the next sprint.
[05:58] Sofia Alvarez: Also, small note - LegacyAI pinned sessions which flattened the tail but increased unit cost significantly. When we simulated pinning with our Dedicated pool, cost went up by about 35% relative to the sticky routing + autoscale approach.
[06:14] Priya Raman: Cost will matter; our procurement will push back if unit cost spikes. Can you provide a cost simulation?
[06:19] Liam Carter: Yes — next step we'll run a cost ladder sim by route with pinning vs sticky routing vs autoscale; we'll include token cost and estimated monthly delta.
[06:28] Ravi Patel: we'll attach an example cost sheet and assumptions.
[06:31] Maya Lopez: About security again: KMS integration - does Redwood support customer-managed keys for both Hosted and Private?
[06:39] Ravi Patel: Customer-managed keys are supported in Private and Dedicated with VPC. For Hosted we offer bring-your-own-key when you move to an enterprise account, but there are additional compliance agreements. We'll outline that in the security doc.
[06:52] Evan Zhao: Any gotchas on audit logs? We need per-token tracing to satisfy regulators, is that possible?
[06:58] Sofia Alvarez: We have request-level audit logs, and you can enable token-level tracing in Private installs; for Hosted it's available with advanced retention add-on. There is a cost and performance consideration — token-level tracing increases I/O and slightly affects latency.
[07:15] Priya Raman: Put that tradeoff in writing.
[07:18] Liam Carter: Will do.
[07:20] Sofia Alvarez: Quick note on the p99 noise: in one run the cluster hit a GPU driver retry which injected spikes; we've marked that as infra noise and excluded it from the final CSV, but we can include the raw run for transparency.
[07:33] Evan Zhao: Good to know.
[07:36] Liam Carter: Alright, next steps recap — we'll share the CSV with per-route buckets, the three flagged samples, cost ladder sim, and the security doc with KMS/SOC2 notes. Sofia will spin up the on-prem quant smoke run once we receive redacted traffic.
[07:54] Priya Raman: Sounds good. Can we schedule the routing thresholds deep dive for next Thursday?
[07:59] Liam Carter: Yep — how about Jan 18th 14:00 UTC?
[08:05] Maya Lopez: Works for me.
[08:07] Evan Zhao: Works.
[08:08] Liam Carter: Perfect, we'll send the invite. Thanks all.
[08:12] Priya Raman: Thanks.
[08:14] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription fidelity: occasional mis-heard acronyms (KV cache sometimes transcribed as 'KV cash'), filler words preserved, and some timestamps approximate.
